original.description: A Belgian Canon de 75 mm modèle 1905 à tir rapide — the Krupp quick-firer built under licence for the Belgian field artillery — in the Gunfire Artilleriemuseum at Brasschaat, the Belgian artillery museum. The Commons record names the object and the museum in one line: "Canon de 75 mle TR (tir rapide Krupp) Gunfire Museum Brasschaat 13-03-2021 10-58-44". It is the TR, the single pole-trail carriage of 1905, and not the split-trail TRA that Belgium rebuilt them into between the wars.
original.date: 13 March 2021 (the photograph); the object is a 75 mm mle 1905 TR, the gun of the Belgian field batteries in August 1914
original.archive: Gunfire Artilleriemuseum, Brasschaat, Belgium (the collection); photograph held on Wikimedia Commons

caption: The Belgian 75 mm mle 1905 à tir rapide, a Krupp quick-firer built under licence, in the Gunfire Artilleriemuseum at Brasschaat. Belgium had it in the field batteries in 1914 and nothing modern behind them.
credit: Photograph: Paul Hermans, 2021, of an object in the Gunfire Artilleriemuseum, Brasschaat; via Wikimedia Commons; CC BY-SA 4.0.
notes: Verified 2026-08-25 against the Commons file record via the MediaWiki API (Artist, Credit, DateTimeOriginal, LicenseShortName, UsageTerms, AttributionRequired read from extmetadata). This is the Belgian field-gun plate the Phase-2 kit pass could not find, and it is also the first Belgian object in the registry that comes from a Belgian museum. The obvious alternative was refused on the date rather than the licence: File:TRA M1905 01.jpg (8000 × 6000, CC BY-SA 3.0) is the same gun in the Royal Museum of the Armed Forces and Military History, Brussels, but its record calls it a TRA — the articulated split-trail carriage Belgium adopted between the wars — so it is not the gun of August 1914 and would have been the same mistake as an M1915 tunic on a 1914 card.
